notes.meaning: After the rebellion at Kadesh-barnea, Israel turned back toward the Red Sea in obedience to God's command. They spent nearly thirty-eight years wandering in the desert around Mount Seir, moving from place to place to find pasture and water. God used this long delay to humble and train a new generation while the older one passed away.

God told Moses that the people had circled the hills of Edom long enough and must now head north toward Canaan. This marked the end of their long years of wandering and the start of their final march to the promised land. When God's appointed time arrives, He calls His people to move forward in faith.

Israel was instructed to travel along the border of Edom, the land belonging to the descendants of Esau, Jacob's twin brother. Because of Israel's great numbers, the Edomites would be terrified of them. God warned Israel to be very careful not to let their strength tempt them into attacking their distant relatives.

The Israelites were forbidden to fight the Edomites or take even a single foot of their land. God had already given the hill country of Mount Seir to Esau's family as their rightful home. True faith respects the boundaries and gifts that God gives to others.

God commanded Israel to pay fair silver prices for all the food and water they received while passing by Edom. Even though God was giving them a daily supply of manna, they were free to buy ordinary provisions whenever available. They were never to use force, theft, or begging to get what they needed.

Moses reminded the people that the Lord had blessed their work, protected their travels, and met all their needs for forty full years. Because God had generously provided for them, they had plenty of silver and had no excuse for dishonesty or robbery. Remembering God's past faithfulness gives His people courage to live honestly.

Israel obeyed the divine instructions and peacefully skirted the borders of their Edomite relatives. They turned away from the southern desert road that ran from the Red Sea ports of Elath and Ezion-geber and headed toward the wilderness east of Moab.

God commanded Moses not to attack or harass the Moabites, promising that Israel would not receive any of their territory. The land of Ar belonged to Moab because they descended from Lot, Abraham's nephew. God honors His ancient kindness to family lines, even when those nations do not know Him well.

Moses noted that a tall, powerful people called the Emites had once lived in the land of Moab. These warriors were counted among the Rephaim, an ancient group known for their great size, much like the Anakites who had frightened Israel's spies. God enabled the Moabites to conquer these giants, showing that sheer human size cannot stand against God's purposes.

In the same way, the Horites used to live in caves in Mount Seir until the descendants of Esau drove them out and took their land. Moses pointed this out so Israel would realize that if God gave land to Edom and Moab, He would certainly give Canaan to His chosen people. The mention of what Israel did looks ahead with total certainty to their upcoming conquest of Canaan.

God ordered the people to get up and cross the Brook of Zered, and they promptly obeyed. Crossing this valley marked the official close of their long desert wanderings and the start of their march into inhabited regions.

Exactly thirty-eight years had passed between Israel's rebellion at Kadesh-barnea and their crossing of the Brook of Zered. During that time, the entire older generation of fighting men died in the desert just as the Lord had sworn. God's hand was actively against them, using special judgments and plagues until all who had refused to trust Him had passed away.

Once the last of that rebellious generation of soldiers had died, the Lord spoke to Moses again. He commanded Israel to cross the border of Moab at the region of Ar on that very day. A fresh generation of faith was now ready to follow God into new territory.

As Israel drew near the territory of the Ammonites, God warned them not to provoke or fight them. Just like Moab, the Ammonites were descendants of Lot, and God had assigned that country to them as their inheritance. God sets the borders of nations, and His people must never take what He has not given them.

The Ammonite land was also once home to giant people known as Rephaim, whom the Ammonites called Zamzummites. Although they were tall and strong like the Anakites, the Lord destroyed them so the Ammonites could settle in their place, just as He did for Esau's family against the Horites. These examples showed Israel that God can bring down any giant before those He chooses to bless.

Moses added that an early people named the Avvim, who lived in small settlements near Gaza, were wiped out by the Caphtorites coming from Caphtor. This historical note showed how God constantly shifts earthly kingdoms and boundaries throughout history.

God commanded Israel to cross the Arnon Valley and begin the battle against Sihon the Amorite, king of Heshbon. Unlike Edom or Moab, the Amorites were wicked and marked for judgment, so God promised to give their land to Israel. On that very day, God would spread panic and dread among all the surrounding nations whenever they heard reports of Israel.

From the wilderness of Kedemoth, Moses sent messengers to King Sihon offering peaceful terms. Israel promised to stay strictly on the main road and pay full price in silver for food and water, just as they had done along the borders of Edom and Moab. This peace offer left Sihon with no excuse when he chose war instead.

King Sihon refused Israel's peaceful request because the Lord made his spirit stubborn and his heart obstinate in order to hand him over to defeat. Sihon willfully rebelled against a fair offer, and God confirmed him in his stubbornness to bring about His just judgment.

differ.view: God actively ordained and governed Sihon's stubbornness as part of His eternal decree to bring judgment, rather than merely watching or passively permitting it.
God did not directly force Sihon's will, but rather allowed or suffered his already wicked heart to harden itself against the truth.

notes.meaning: The Lord told Moses that the defeat of Sihon had officially begun and urged Israel to take possession of the Amorite territory. Even though victory was guaranteed by promise, the people still had to step out and fight.
Sihon marched out with his entire army to fight Israel at Jahaz. The Lord gave Israel the victory, enabling them to strike down Sihon, his sons, and all his forces in battle.

Israel captured every city and devoted the entire population to destruction, leaving no survivors among the men, women, or children. This extreme destruction was carried out as a direct command from God to execute His holy judgment on the Amorites for their deep, unrepented wickedness. The Israelites were permitted to keep only the farm animals and the material goods as plunder.

Israel took all the land from Aroer on the rim of the Arnon Valley all the way up to Gilead. Not a single fortified city had walls too high or too strong for them, because the Lord fought for them and delivered everything into their hands. What had terrified the earlier generation became an easy victory when they trusted God.

Throughout this campaign, Israel carefully obeyed God by staying away from the land belonging to the Ammonites, the river Jabbok, and the mountain towns. Even in the thrill of military victory, God's people kept strictly within the boundaries He had commanded.
